stagedirection
speechtext:
The house in committee on Bill No. 16, respecting certain patent applications owned by the British Steel Piling Company, Limited -Mr. Jacobs-Mr. Johnston in the chair.
On section 1-Authority to issue patents notwithstanding delay in filing applications.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Let us have some explanation with respect to this.

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext:
The bill is similar to the one just passed, and it stands in the name of the hon. member for Cartier (Mr. Jacobs). It was referred to committee, and after explanations had been given certain amendments were made. On page 2 of the bill, line 6, after the word "shall," the following words were inserted in the first section:
.... notwithstanding anything contained in the Patent Act, date from the seventeenth day of May, 1923, and the seventeenth day of May, 1924, respectively, and shall-

-in the period between the seventeenth day of February, 1924-

I did not quite catch what the hon. gentleman said. Did he say these amendments had been before the*committee?

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext: I think they were.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
I might explain that the same reservation is made as in the previous bill. In this case the patents concerned were obtained in Great Britain by the holders but they had failed to register in Canada within the period of one year as required by the act. They are now coming to us to file their patents in Canada. We could not, however, grant the patents under the act; a special bill is required to enable them to obtain registration in Canada. The amendments that my hon. friend has mentioned are in the same class as those in the previous bill, the effect being to take the patents from the date on which application should have been made

Ways and Means-Customs Tariff
rather than this year. If any person has in the intervening period manufactured, used or sold in Canada the inventions described, then such person may continue to manufacture, use or sell such inventions in Canada. This is the customary clause, but our information in the department is that nothing of the kind has happened. Again I say that we are in the hands of the committee. The department as such does not. recommend any bill of the kind.
But the private bills committee did make these amendments?

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext: Yes, the amendments which I read.
Because it is asserted they did, and the chairman apparently says they did not.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: I may say to my hon. friend that we made two amendments.

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext: The amendments which I read.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: The first as to the date of the issue of the patent, and the second for the protection of the vested rights.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: The amendment is being made to the section in the terms mentioned by the hon. member for Dorchester (Mr. Cannon) ?

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext: Exactly.

speakerposition: stagedirection

Section agreed to.
Sections 2 and 3 agreed to.

speechtext: The house in committee of ways and means, Mr. Johnston in the chair.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: When the house rose at six o'clock, we were considering item 522d.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Does the adding of this item in any way change the existing conditions? I understand it does not.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It is just adding the word "mercerized".

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Provided that the manufacturers manufacture it in their own factories.
Are the rates under this item the same as the rates under the original 522d?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No, they are free in all three columns. We have added the word "mercerised".
What is the effect of this?

Does a different class oi manufacturer use the goods or what is the reason for the difference in the duty? Is it a question of protection to one manufacturer as opposed to another? My point is that manufacturers use both. Why then should one manufacturer be able to import 40's and finer, mercerized, free, and the other have to pay a duty if he imports?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
These mercerized yarns are
not widely made in Canada.
Item agreed' to.
Customs tariff-522e. Yarns wholly of cotton, exceeding number twenty, and not exceeding number forty, not more advanced than singles; cotton sewing thread yarn and crochet, knitting, darning and embroidery yarn, in hanks, composed of three strands or more, not bleached, coloured nor mercerized; imported by manufacturers who manufacture cotton sewing thread and crochet, knitting, darning and embroidery cottons only for use exclusively in their own factories in the manufacture of those materials: British preferential tariff, 7i per cent; intermediate tariff, 15 per cent; general tariff, 20 per cent.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I beg to move that the following be substituted for tariff item 522e:
522e. Yarns wholly of cotton, exceeding number twenty, and not exceeding number forty, not more advanced than singles; cotton sewing thread yarn and crochet, knitting, darning and embroidery yarn, in hanks, composed of tw:o strands or more; all yarns specified in this item when imported by manufacturers for use exclusively in their own factories in the manufacturing or spooling of cotton sewing thread and crochet, knitting, darning arid embroidery cottons: British preferential tariff, 7J per cent; intermediate tariff, 15 per cent; general tariff, 20 per cent.
This item is a grouping of a number of items?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It is a grouping of items 520, 525 and 536.

The minister will pardon me if I am not quite clear, but I will read the first part of item 522e:
Yarns wholly of cotton, exceeding number twenty, and not exceeding number forty, not more advanced than singles.
Item number 522a reads:
Yarns .	.	.	. wholly of cotton, exceeding
number twenty, but not exceeding number forty, not more advanced than singles.
Why repeat this in the composite item when it is provided for in item 522a? The reason

Ways and Means-Customs Tariff
I draw attention to that is this: In the old tariff it was pointed out by the minister that certain articles were entered under one item when perhaps they should have been under another; that this earned considerable confusion and that the change was supposed to clear it up. Now we have a repetition of two items with a difference in the rate of duty. If I am wrong I wish the minister would point out where I am wrong or make an explanation.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: This is a manufacturers' item. The other was a consumers' item.
Then the consumers' item bears a duty of 12| per cent, 15 per cent and 22| per cent, and the manufacturers' item bears a duty of 7j per cent, 15 per cent and 20 per cent. Is that right?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
Is there no method of
overcoming the difficulty that has been experienced in the customs department with re-peet to articles that are imported for use of manufacturers only in their own mills and that are very often sold out of stock and used elsewhere? As the minister knows, there has been a good deal of discussion as to how the public can be safeguarded in connection with matters of that kind where you specify, as I said yesterday, the place at which the article is to be used and the conditions under which the usage takes place.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is effected by the different changes. The customs officials have approved this and they believe they will be able to work it out.
I notice the original draft reads, " three strands or more," and the present one reads, "Two strands or more." What is the object of the amendment?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: This is to broaden out the administration of the act.
I am asking why the minister is decreasing the number of strands.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: This allows them to get two strands or more. It was felt that to make it three strands was a little strict. The manufacturers have asked for this change.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: What is the effect of it?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I imagine the effect of it is to make it a little easier for the manufacturers to get the raw product they require. It was found that some of them were using two-ply and doubling them.

I understand we are discussing item 522e. The conversation across the floor has been in such a low tone that I could not hear it. I notice cotton yams were dutiable at 15 per cent. 22^ per cent and 25 per cent. This is about the sixth or seventh reference to item 522, and it looks as though we are getting a cut of about 7i per cent in the duty, but I wonder if the minister can give us any idea of the amount of imports that will be affected, that came in under the (wo rates last year. How much of a reduction is it-one per cent or a fraction of one per cent? V hat will be the possible loss of revenue?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
There is a portion under
several of the other items, and I cannot tell; but under item 535 the importations amounted to $636,628.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Item agreed to.
Customs tariff-522f.	Yarns and warps
wholly of cotton imported by manufacturers of tapes, braids, webbings and woven labels for use exclusively in the manufacture of such articles in their own factories:	Provided that yarns and warps which are entitled to free entry or to lower rates than are mentioned in this item shall not be entered at the rate specified in this item: British preferential tariff, 7J per cent; intermediate tariff, 12£ per cent; general tariff, 15 per cent.
Is this in order? We have before us the votes and proceedings of February 16, and in my copy there is no item 522f. Can we go on with it under those conditions?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: These are goods that are procurable in Canada and that are used by manufacturers.
The point is that the committee has had no notice of this.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I do not Object to having it go on the record and letting it stand so that my hon. friends can examine it.
Do I understand the minister to say that the item will stand?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I have no objection, if the committee insists upon it.

Perhaps the minister could explain something in the meantime. The item states:
Provided that yarns and warps which are entitled to free entry or to lower rates than are mentioned in this item shall not be entered at the rates specified in this item.
Does that mean that yarns and warps now entering free, if they come under the terms of this item, shall not be subject to this duty?

1436	COMMONS
Ways and Means-Customs Tariff

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: If they are entitled to free entry under another item, they will still be free.
I see, and it is only in ease of a higher duty under some other item that this change takes place.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is right.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: There arises here a difficulty which I trust the Minister of National Revenue will consider. I have received communications of late with respect to the administration of the Customs Act and with respect to changes made by orders in council of which the public is not aware. A man buys goods, pays his duty, sells them, and then an order in council is passed by which the classification is in some sense altered, and he is called upon to pay additional duties sometimes exceeding the profit he madia with respect to the transaction. Then the old difficulty arises; he gets his friends in parliament or at Ottawa to work for him, while somebody else who is not so fortunate is left out in the cold. That actually happened in connection with a rather important transaction at one of the ports recently. The point made by the hon. member for Argen-teuil is very important here. If these amendments are to be made, from what date are they to apply? These are absolutely new items, as the minister was good enough to say. Will the importers who brought in their goods under the old items as they stood prior to the date of to-day or to-morrow, or whatever day the minister fixes, be called upon to pay under the new or the old item, and will they be entitled to a refund if they paid at a higher rate than is mentioned here? As it stands, of course, they all go back to the date of the budget speech, but these new items were not brought down until yesterday.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
My hon. friend will observe that it is governed by this provision:
This act shall be deemed to have come into force on the seventeenth day of February, one thousand nine hundred and twenty-eight, and to have applied to all goods mentioned in the foreging resolution imported or taken out of warehouse for consumption on and after that date and to have applied to goods previously imported for which no entry for consumption was made before that day.

How, then, can the minister justify bringing in these alterations without notice, proposing to pass new items and have them take effect as if they had been brought in on the 16th day of February when he made his budget speech? How can he justify that without giving notice to anybody?
4,Vtr K. J. Garland.]

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
That has always been the
procedure, and under alii governments, I think.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
In the case of slight
amendments, but not new items.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
This is a reduction. As to
the point raised by my hon. friend a moment ago regarding increased duties, I do not see how that could possibly arise because, as he knows, the government cannot increase the duty by order in council.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: I was speaking of classification, determining in what class a given article shall come. I will give my hon. friend a concrete case if he so desires. Only to-day while I was in the chamber a telephone message was left at the office saying that the Journals were not as full as they have been heretofore with respect to these items. I do not know what was meant by that because I was not there, but evidently it was these items that were in mind. My hon. friend should give notice so that the public will know exactly where they stand. As far as I personally am concerned, it is not a matter of importance, and as far as my friend from South Wellington is concerned it is not a matter of importance to him, but, after all, the public have rights, and I think we had better consider them according to the rules of parliament.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
In the administration of the
act the board of customs from time to time do reclassify goods.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: And make the classification retroactive; that is the trouble.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
This is not a new procedure
at all. I observe, for instance, that in 1920 there were 25 changes made after the resolutions were brought down.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
Some of them merely
typographical changes.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I have not gone through
them, but that has been the procedure.

Will the minister inform
the committee what the practice is to be? The act comes into force and the new rates of duty are applied from the 17th of February. So far as the public are concerned, they have no notice of any changes or of any new items. New items can only be considered in the ordinary way, and notice should be given of them in the Votes and Proceedings. When will these new items take effect? Do they date back to the 17th of February or become effective from the day they are introduced?

speechtext: Under the procedure that has always been followed in the past, from the day the budget is brought down the customs officers take all entries under the new items, subject to any amendments.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
And subject, of course,
to rebate in case the duty is lowered, or a further charge if it is increased.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I do not object to its standing if hon. gentlemen insist upon it.

It is a
decrease. I do not ask that it stand.

speechtext: Any changes here?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: There is no change. This is the resolution as brought down.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Is there any change from the old tariff?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes. The rates proposed under this classification are 12^, 20 and 22J per cent. The former rates were, under item 521, 12J, 22i and 25 per cent; item 524, 15, 17i and 20 per cent; item 524b, 15, 17i and 20 per cent. The imports for the year ending March 31, 1927, were, under item 521, 1617,537 British preference; $6,557 treaty rates; $1,199,223 general tariff; item 524, $60,486 British preference; none under treaty rates; $501,894 general tariff; item 524b, $454 British preference; $446,987 general tariff. And an increase in the general rate.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: There is an increase in the general rate on two items, but the importations were largely under item 521.

I would like to point out to the minister something that might help us in studying these matters. I have here the volume, Trade of Canada, and in a general way one can tell where a certain item comes in this volume but if it contained a column alongside the description of the various classes giving the number of the tariff item concerned, you could tell exactly under which item the imports were entering. As it is at present, the descriptions contained in this volume do not correspond with the descriptions in the tariff schedules, and no item numbers are
given. If the number of the item were included opposite the description of the goods, we could get from this volume a proper check of the imports.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
That is a very important
point, and I believe under the new classification they might be able to follow it more closely. I shall direct it to the attention of the Bureau of Statistics.

The minister said a few
minutes ago that there was a decrease from 15 to 12J per cent on these items under the general tariff. The amount of importations was about $6,500. There is an increase there-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Before my hon. friend proceeds further I will give him the correct figures. The amounts under item 521?
No, items 524 and 524b.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Item 524, $60,486, and item
524b, $4,054, under the British preference.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: About that.

And under the general
tariff, which is increased 2i per cent, you have importations of $950,000. That certainly is decreasing the tariff!

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
My hon. friend has not
observed that the policy is to divert as much as possible of that business to the United Kingdom. This will be sufficient to divert it to the British industries.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
Surely my hon. friend
is not serious in that.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: What more does my hon. friend want?

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
Great Britain does not
produce raw cotton; the United States does. Great Britain is separated from Canada by 3,000 miles of ocean; the United States adjoins us. Yet he wants the committee to believe that a change of but 2\ per cent is going to divert the traffic to Great Britain from the United States, whence at the present moment we are getting $950,000 worth, as against only $65,000 worth from Great Britain.

All the afternoon I have
heard the argument about changing the British preference 2| per cent to increase imports from Great Britain. Now, my experience in mercantile business leads me to believe that it will do nothing of the kind. What controls the buying of goods more than anything else is quick turnover and proximity of market.

Ways and Means-Customs Tariff
The minister admitted that this afternoon.

I say this change will not
divert the business to Great Britain because the American market is close to us. The object of all general mercantile business today is to increase its turnover. Naturally the closer your market the quicker you get your goods and the greater your turnover. When you come to the practical effect of this change, I say in my opinion it will increase business with the United States instead of with Great Britain.

I do not
think there is the least doubt in the world that the statement of the last speaker can be supported by the figures given by the minister, as well as by a general consideration of the items. Let me put it to him in this way, and I am going to be even more severe than the hon. member for Cariboo (Mr. Fraser) :	Not only will the trade not be
diverted to England, but I think the minister's explanation is most insincere; I do not think he is under any delusion in the matter at all. If he is really interested in diverting the trade to British manufacturers, let him put this on the free list with Britain. Then we will believe the minister. But when he says there is a reduction of duty because of the 2i per cent increase in the British preference, well, he is asking the committee to believe a whole lot more than we are capable of. Will the minister consider putting it on the free list?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
No. It is thought that this
is a fair reclassification. It is also believed that the 2} per cent additional advantage is worth while to the British manufacturers.

The minister, I suppose,
realizes that the whole effect of the change is an increase in customs duty? That is the result that we will have.
Absolutely.

On our large importations from the United States the rate is increased. On a comparatively negligible part of our imports, $65,000 worth, the rate is lowered 2J per cent, but on the aggregate under this item more will be collected by the department. The rate of duty is higher. That is the result of these tariff changes on this particular item.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
No. Had my hon. friend
figured it out he would not have made that statement. I have the figures here of the estimated changes in taxation based on the imports of last year. Under tariff item 521 there will be a decrease of $30,146; under

tariff item 524, an increase of $11,035; under tariff item 524b, an increase of $11,163-or a net decrease of $7,948.
I cannot understand it.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Not on the facts stated.

One of the previous
items, I think 522b, was given free entry under the British preference. I remember last night asking the minister about an increase in the intermediate and general tariffs on one of the other items, and he explained that the increase was due to the fact that they wanted to increase the rate proportionately under the intermediate and general tariff and still maintain the item free under the British preference. Under this item 521, cotton fabrics unbleached, according to the Trade of Canada, page 170, we imported from the United Kingdom 7,000,000 yards, and from the United States 13,000,000 yards. In this item there is a reduction of 2^ per cent in the general tariff applying to the United States; there is no reduction in the preferential tariff applying to the United Kingdom. There is a change in principle in that arrangement. Would the minister explain why there is no reduction in the British preference in this instance? I understood last night that he was anxious to maintain the British preference.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

speechtext: Good Lord! For a preferential rate 12i per cent is not a low, it is a high rate. The minister, I think, has not yet got the point of the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Kennedy). The minister cannot really be serious. The United Kingdom exported to us 7,000,000 yards, according to the last trade figures; the United States, 13,000,000 yards. But uhder this item the preference remains the same, that is, the United Kingdom traders get no particular advantage; but there is a decrease to the American manufacturer of 2J per cent under the intermediate.

The minister must realize how misleading these figures are; they have no relevancy at all. We have a new item in this tariff. We have fabrics wholly of cotton, n.o.p. You may be providing for items that were not provided for in the old tariff and the real result is a substantial increase. Let me put it this way:	You have
cotton fabrics of all kinds and you specify the rates of duty at which, say, 90 out of 100 parcels shall be dealt with. The remaining 10 not having been specifically mentioned are dealt with under the n.o.p. provisions. Before this tariff was introduced you dealt with, say, fifty or sixty of the hundred articles specifically, while the n.o.p. clause applied to the other forty. I contend that you cannot institute any comparison between those forty and the ten to which I have referred. As I say, this item really amounts to a substantial increase in the tariff.

speechtext: My hon. friend is right when he says that there is a general reclassification, but we must consider these items all together. To-day, taking the total changes in the schedules, there will be an aggregate decrease of $1,119,560.

But you are comparing
different things.

speechtext:
I agree with my hon. friend

That is excellent publicity, but it is not very convincing. I have before me two items. Item 523b of the new tariff gives the rates as 20, 25 and 27i; under item 522 of the old tariff they are 15, 22i and 25.

speechtext: The former rates were 22k, 30 and 32i; they are now 20, 25 and 27|.

speechtext:
I have given printed cotton

Those are general figures. Gam the minister give us the importations and the reduction in revenue under that one item, 638, buckram, which is now free of duty?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I am not sure that I have it handy.
If it is free of duty how do you get revenue out of it at all? Can the minister give us 523, cotton fabrics, dyed?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is the one I have been quoting. I gave the importations as $1,896,147.
What would be the estimated loss in revenue as a result of the decrease under the joint item now called 523b.

speechtext:
Buckram is one of the items
subject to the 99 per cent drawback.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition

Is there or is there not an increase in the item?

speechtext:
No, a decrease; I have repeated

What is the decrease in connection with buckram?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: There are two items that come under this one. One shows a decrease of $69,273, and the other a decrease of $184,695.

Which is
which? I cannot understand that at all. The minister says there are two items, but certainly there cannot be reductions in both of them. How can that be when one is free?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The buckram about which my hon. friend is speaking goes into another classification; it will be entitled to a drawback of 99 per cent.

There seems to be a mistake in this somewhere. If you look at item 523b and go right across the page you come to buckram; under item 523c, if you go right across the page you come to cotton fabrics, and there is a bracket which includes buckram and cotton fabrics, which is very confusing. If the minister will look at that he will possibly see the difficulty. Under the old schedules buckram and cotton fabrics did not seem to belong to the one item at all. That seems to be where we are all confused.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
Yes, and I think if the hon. member for Peace River will look at item 1061 he will accentuate that point. The minister said buckram was being given a drawback, although heretofore it has been free. Item 1061 includes:
Woven fabrics for book binding.
On this item there is a drawback of 99 per cent, so there is an increase of at least one per cent, whatever else may be said of it.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: There is a drawback.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: A drawback of 99 per cent.
How do you get a drawback on an article coming in free?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The old item was:
Buckram, adapted for the manufacture of hat and bonnet shapes.
Under that classification it was free, but under the new item it is placed as a drawback item.
The minister is not quite right. The drawback is granted where this is brought in as bookbinding material only, unless you have another item.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Also for hats and bonnets.
What item is that?
Item 1012.
Is buckram a cotton product?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes, I think it is in that classification.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: It is not cotton at all; as a matter of fact it is linen.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
In answer to my hon. friend for Vanceuver Centre, (Mr. Stevens), when we come to it the new item will read:
When used in the manufacture of linings for hats and caps of in the manufacture of hat shapes and bonnet shapes from buckram.
There is an amendment to be made?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: But what is the duty which will be imposed in order that the drawback way be made?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
If it comes in as an n.o.p.
article it may come as coloured linings or as coloured cottons.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: And if so, there is a drawback of 99 per cent? Then an item which was free before you tinkered with the tariff is now subject to a drawback of 99 per cent; in other words the duty is increased by one per cent.
What is the advantage of making a free article dutiable and then handing back 99 per cent?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: For administrative purposes.

If the minister will tell us how that is going to simplify matters I shall be tickled to death. It is now free; there is no administrative work in connection with it, but we are going to place a duty on it which will necessitate custom houses, inspections and appraisals, and then we are giving a drawback of 99 per cent which will require a staff to look after it. And the minister says it will simplify the work.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The customs department asked for this change originally. I will be frank with my hon. friends; this is one of the items which, as we have been taught by experience, have been abused.
Will you not have the same difficulty whether it comes in free or whether it is taxed?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
One does not wish to
worry -the minister unnecessarily, but I put this to him faMy: He is going to increase the work of the people in the customs department, which means more employees and a greater cost to the people. The article must go through the customs; duty must be ipaid, and 99 per cent of the money must be returned. The unfortunate taxpayer is out his money; he has to pay the duty and then wait until he gets a cheque back for the drawback to which' he is entitled. Then, in the item as it formerly stood, buckram came in free and simply had to be passed through the customs. Now it wild be charged a duty of only one per cent, and considerable machinery will be required to do the additional work. That is the sum total of this change, and we are told that someone wants the change for administrative purposes. I never saw a chance to make another job, where the public service is affected, in which some person did not want to make the necessary change. I am sorry to say that is so.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I will admit that that condition prevails more or less.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: My hon. friend knows that; he has had more experience than I have had. I do not see why we should make this change, which will be an expense to the country, and which will only mean the collection of a duty of one per cent.

I think this item could be very well compared to that item which referred to shoe laces; there may be abuses of this item also. Buckram may be used for purposes for whioh it should not be admitted free. Now, hat manufacturers and bookbinders will receive a refund on the buckram they use while everyone else will have to pay a duty.
Then this is an increase in the duty.
No. These other people h,we been getting it under false pretences.

How could they be
getting it under false pretences when it is free? How could there be any evasion of duty there? You are now specifying that only certain people will receive a drawback, and you reduce the principle of favoritism as between the manufacturers of different articles. That must be the purpose.

You will find a great difference if you ask for a drawback; you will deal with an expert who looks after these things. When you are simply clearing an article through customs you often deal with
men who have not a great deal of experience, who consider the invoice more than the quality of the goods.
Where could the abuse arise in connection with a free article coming into the country for commercial purposes?

My understanding of this matter is that buckram for the manufacture of hats and for use in bookbinding comes in free, but we must remember that buckram is also used in the manufacture of clothing. The effect of this tariff change, as I see it, is to put a duty on buckram used foi the purpose of stiffening for clothing, so that people who buy clothes wil have to pay the duty, while those buying hats will not have to pay it.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: My hon. friend has just proved the case; if he is right there has been an abuse. Under the old item it was not intended that the buckram should be used for anything except what was stated. Manufacturers of clothing have a certain protection, and they are entitled to pay for that particular protection. My hon. friends are wrong in saying that this comes in for bookbinding. Bookbinding is under another item.
If the material is for the manufacture of a suit of clothes it is probably dutiable.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The manufacturer of clothes never had the privilege which my hon. friend says he has been using or abusing.

I did not say anything
about it. I say that under the old act it is absolutely free.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
No. Let me read the old
tariff and my hon. friend can place his own interpretation upon it. It is:
Buckram, adapted for the manufacture of hat and bonnet shapes.
The manufacturers may have brought it in and used it for other purposes but it never was intended that they should.

When coming in through Canadian ports.

wholly of cotton, not to include horse blankets, automobile or steamer rugs, nor similar articles: British preferential tariff. 15 per cent; intermediate tariff, 22J per cent; general tariff, 27J per cent.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The former rates were 22| per cent, 30 per cent and 35 per cent. The imports for the year ended 31st March, 1927, were $252,154 and the estimated reduction in taxation is $19,061.

This is an item which directly concerns every family in the land. Under another item we have made a kind of cotton duck entirely free. I do not see why the government should discriminate between one class and another all the way through this schedule. They say that the cotton industry languishes because there is not work. It languishes simply because the buying power of our working people throughout the country is being everlastingly curtailed by these measures Not only is the amount of duty added to the value of the goods, but at the same time about two dollars goes into the pockets of the manufacturer for every dollar that goes into the Dominion treasury. As I say, this is a commodity that is used by every family in the land and yet we maintain almost the highest rate of duty on it. It is a commodity that everyone that is working and producing for a living has to buy. This is
a most unfair and discriminatory principle from beginning to end and I wish to make that protest on this item.

Could the minister tell us why horse bankets are excluded? I have a vivid picture in my mind of something I saw about two months ago, of a farmer, when it was fifty degrees below zero, leaving for a twenty-mile trip with six horses and two hundred bushels of wheat. Anybody who has lived in western Canada and knows anything about pioneering, realizes how important a horse blanket is. It seems to me that some consideration might be given to the people who want to use horse blankets and who have to do the difficult pioneering work in which this commodity is used to such a large extent. If we are going to do anything about settling up the new districts, there will always be a big demand for horse blankets, and most of those who are dealing in horse blankets are doing pretty well.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: My hon. friend knows that horse blankets are not generally made of cotton. They are largely made of jute and they come under another item.
Why are they excluded from this item?

speechtext:
Because this is household
blankets.

All waterproof horse blankets are made of cotton duck and they should be included in this item. We are dealing with cotton. Horse blankets of jute are made for cold, dry weather.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

Cotton horse blankets still come in at the high rate. speechtext:
But he uses jute.

This item covers socks and
stockings. This again is a workingman's article. The wage earner uses this very class of socks and stockings. It is a mistaken policy to try to build up industry in this country by bleeding the workingman. It is a fallacy in economics to tax the workingman for the sake of providing dividends for big cotton companies such as were mentioned this afternoon, which are already in a prosperous condition. If Canada is ever going to be anything, it will depend on keeping down the cost of living, and I submit to the government that it would be much better to lower the cost of living than to have our workingmen striking for higher wages all the time. This article is a necessity, one of the very necessities Of life, and why not begin here? Why tax the workingman for the benefit of the millionaire?-for that is what we are doing by this item. The working classes have to use this kind of socks and1 stockings, and there is no reason why we should put a 271 per cent duty on this article.

For instance, hammocks, tennis nets, sportsmen's fishing nets, oiled silk, oiled cloth, oiled tape and other textiles, India rubber coats, corsets of all kinds, linen and cotton clothing, window shade cloth, window shades cut to size, hemmed and mounted on rollers, and so on.
